title: The Best Thing You Can Do Before the School Year Starts Has Nothing to Do With Curriculum
author: Shari Keller
summary: Shari Keller argues that the most consequential preparation homeschooling parents can do before the school year isn't choosing curriculum but examining their own relationship to learning, since 'your kids don't read your lesson plans, they read you.' She grounds this in a personal failure: pulling her son out of a discouraging kindergarten only to hand him a carefully chosen curriculum he still resisted, because she had answered the wrong question — 'what do I teach him' instead of 'how do I mentor this specific kid.' Her sharpest example concerns grammar, which she dreaded teaching not because it was hard but because her own schooling had made it tedious and disconnected — dread she was unconsciously transmitting to her children until she taught grammar in service of her daughter's own stories instead of as an isolated subject. Keller frames unscheduled 'rabbit trail' learning (a pirate story leading to a globe, snacks, and an outdoor pirate-ship lunch) as evidence that following genuine curiosity beats executing a preset plan, and closes with three self-examination questions for parents to ask before September: what subjects do I approach with dread and where did that come from, do I check my own assumptions before pushing a stuck child forward, and am I willing to keep learning and changing my mind alongside my kid.
points: Keller's central reframe — 'your kids don't read your lesson plans, they read you... your relationship to learning is the first curriculum your child encounters' — relocates the highest-leverage preparation from materials selection to parental self-examination.

Her grammar example demonstrates a specific, transferable mechanism: unexamined dread from a parent's own schooling gets unconsciously transmitted to a child, and the fix wasn't a better curriculum but reframing grammar as a service to the child's own writing rather than an isolated subject.
The distinction she draws between 'what do I teach him' and 'how do I actually mentor this specific kid' gives parents a concrete diagnostic question to ask before finalizing any curriculum plan.

Her three pre-September questions (what do I dread and why, do I check my own assumptions before pushing a stuck child, am I willing to keep learning alongside them) function as a reusable self-audit any teaching parent — not only homeschoolers — could apply.
quotes: Somewhere underneath all of that is a question you probably haven't said out loud: What if I don't know enough to do this well?
Even though I believed strongly in project based and experiential learning, I had bought into the idea that the right materials would do the work.
Your kids don't read your lesson plans. They read you. They notice whether you find something genuinely interesting or whether you're pushing through it because it's on the schedule.
That dread was mine. My kids didn't come with it. But I was handing it to them anyway.
Grammar as its own subject wasn't working. Grammar in the service of a story she actually cared about? Completely different.
You start to catch yourself sooner — when the resistance in the room is coming from your kid, and when it's coming from you.
The parents who do this well aren't the ones who knew the most at the start. They're the ones who stayed open to learning on the job.
The best preparation you can do this August has nothing to do with curriculum. It's deciding to be a learner yourself — right alongside your kid, from day one.
